2|name: arc-grid-reasoning
3|description: Use for ARC-style colored-grid puzzle solving.
4|---
5|
6|# ARC grid reasoning
7|
8|Use this skill for ARC-style tasks with colored integer grids and a small number of input/output demonstrations. Infer the simplest rule that explains every demonstrated change, then apply it exactly to the test grid.
9|
10|## Workflow
11|
12|1. **Preserve the interaction contract.** If the environment requires one action per turn (submit/request_demo/finish), emit exactly one valid action object in the required location. Do not add explanatory text when the protocol requires JSON-only. Respect attempt and demo caps.
13|2. **Parse the grid before hypothesizing.** Record dimensions, background color, connected components by color (usually 4-connectivity; also inspect diagonal relationships), bounding boxes, shapes, and repeated motifs. Watch for objects touching the boundary or separated by only one background cell.
14|3. **Use demonstrations as before/after diffs.** For every demo, identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed invariant. Group changed cells into components; note whether objects are recolored, moved, copied, extended, or deleted. Never summarize an entire demo as a vague scene description.
15|4. **Infer candidate rules from relations, not just resemblance.** Compare the changed object against unchanged objects of the same color/shape. Test plausible selectors (orientation, position relative to an anchor, size, shape, count, alignment, enclosure, matching dimensions) against all demos. Explicitly identify counterexamples and eliminate hypotheses that fail them.
16|5. **Treat multiple demos as constraints.** The rule should explain each example with the same mechanism, allowing only task-intrinsic variation such as colors, orientations, or object positions. If two explanations remain plausible and would yield different test outputs, ask for another demo when its expected value exceeds its cost.
17|6. **Request demonstrations strategically.** A demo request costs one point, but a wrong submission also costs one and an unsolved instance may incur the full budget. Ask when it can distinguish specific live hypotheses; avoid requesting merely for reassurance after the rule is already strongly constrained. Before requesting, state internally which outcomes would confirm/reject each candidate.
18|7. **Apply transformations minimally.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and alter only cells compelled by the inferred rule. Preserve dimensions and all unrelated pixels. Use a small script or carefully indexed representation for large grids; check row lengths and changed-cell coordinates before submission.
19|8. **Verify the final action.** Confirm dimensions, allowed values, exact row count and width, and that unchanged regions match the input. If submitting, output exactly one action with a valid grid. Do not claim correctness until the environment confirms it.
20|
21|## Common pitfalls
22|
23|- **Premature pattern naming:** an L-shaped marker and nearby object may suggest a familiar rule, but proximity alone is weak evidence. Compare with similar unchanged candidates.
24|- **Ignoring changed-cell precision:** output examples often differ at just one component; changing too much is a common failure.
25|- **Single-example overfit:** a rule that fits one demo may not generalize; leverage additional demos to distinguish selection from coincidence.
26|- **Coordinate drift:** grids are often wide or tall; keep row/column indexing consistent (state whether zero- or one-based) and validate dimensions mechanically where practical.
27|- **Tool overhead:** parallel analysis can help on genuinely ambiguous hypotheses, but repeated status checks and redundant delegation do not improve the puzzle evidence. Prefer independent, bounded analyses that return a concrete candidate and rationale.
28|
29|## Support reference

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks with colored integer grids and a small number of input/output demonstrations. Infer the simplest rule that explains every demonstrated change, then apply it exactly to the test grid.

## Workflow

1. **Preserve the interaction contract.** If the environment requires one action per turn (submit/request_demo/finish), emit exactly one valid action object in the required location. Do not add explanatory text when the protocol requires JSON-only. Respect attempt and demo caps.
2. **Parse the grid before hypothesizing.** Record dimensions, background color, connected components by color (usually 4-connectivity; also inspect diagonal relationships), bounding boxes, shapes, and repeated motifs. Watch for objects touching the boundary or separated by only one background cell.
3. **Use demonstrations as before/after diffs.** For every demo, identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed invariant. Group changed cells into components; note whether objects are recolored, moved, copied, extended, or deleted. Never summarize an entire demo as a vague scene description.
4. **Infer candidate rules from relations, not just resemblance.** Compare the changed object against unchanged objects of the same color/shape. Test plausible selectors (orientation, position relative to an anchor, size, shape, count, alignment, enclosure, matching dimensions) against all demos. Explicitly identify counterexamples and eliminate hypotheses that fail them.
5. **Treat multiple demos as constraints.** The rule should explain each example with the same mechanism, allowing only task-intrinsic variation such as colors, orientations, or object positions. If two explanations remain plausible and would yield different test outputs, ask for another demo when its expected value exceeds its cost.
6. **Request demonstrations strategically.** A demo request costs one point, but a wrong submission also costs one and an unsolved instance may incur the full budget. Ask when it can distinguish specific live hypotheses; avoid requesting merely for reassurance after the rule is already strongly constrained. Before requesting, state internally which outcomes would confirm/reject each candidate.
7. **Apply transformations minimally.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and alter only cells compelled by the inferred rule. Preserve dimensions and all unrelated pixels. Use a small script or carefully indexed representation for large grids; check row lengths and changed-cell coordinates before submission.
8. **Verify the final action.** Confirm dimensions, allowed values, exact row count and width, and that unchanged regions match the input. If submitting, output exactly one action with a valid grid. Do not claim correctness until the environment confirms it.

## Common pitfalls

- **Premature pattern naming:** an L-shaped marker and nearby object may suggest a familiar rule, but proximity alone is weak evidence. Compare with similar unchanged candidates.
- **Ignoring changed-cell precision:** output examples often differ at just one component; changing too much is a common failure.
- **Single-example overfit:** a rule that fits one demo may not generalize; leverage additional demos to distinguish selection from coincidence.
- **Coordinate drift:** grids are often wide or tall; keep row/column indexing consistent (state whether zero- or one-based) and validate dimensions mechanically where practical.
- **Tool overhead:** parallel analysis can help on genuinely ambiguous hypotheses, but repeated status checks and redundant delegation do not improve the puzzle evidence. Prefer independent, bounded analyses that return a concrete candidate and rationale.

## Support reference

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks with colored integer grids and a small number of input/output demonstrations. Infer the simplest rule that explains every demonstrated change, then apply it exactly to the test grid.

## Workflow

1. **Preserve the interaction contract.** If the environment requires one action per turn (submit/request_demo/finish), emit exactly one valid action object in the required location. Do not add explanatory text when the protocol requires JSON-only. Respect attempt and demo caps.
2. **Parse the grid before hypothesizing.** Record dimensions, background color, connected components by color (usually 4-connectivity; also inspect diagonal relationships), bounding boxes, shapes, and repeated motifs. Watch for objects touching the boundary or separated by only one background cell.
3. **Use demonstrations as before/after diffs.** For every demo, identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed invariant. Group changed cells into components; note whether objects are recolored, moved, copied, extended, or deleted. Never summarize an entire demo as a vague scene description.
4. **Infer candidate rules from relations, not just resemblance.** Compare the changed object against unchanged objects of the same color/shape. Test plausible selectors (orientation, position relative to an anchor, size, shape, count, alignment, enclosure, matching dimensions) against all demos. Explicitly identify counterexamples and eliminate hypotheses that fail them.
5. **Treat multiple demos as constraints.** The rule should explain each example with the same mechanism, allowing only task-intrinsic variation such as colors, orientations, or object positions. If two explanations remain plausible and would yield different test outputs, ask for another demo when its expected value exceeds its cost.
6. **Request demonstrations strategically.** A demo request costs one point, but a wrong submission also costs one and an unsolved instance may incur the full budget. Ask when it can distinguish specific live hypotheses; avoid requesting merely for reassurance after the rule is already strongly constrained. Before requesting, state internally which outcomes would confirm/reject each candidate.
7. **Apply transformations minimally.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and alter only cells compelled by the inferred rule. Preserve dimensions and all unrelated pixels. Use a small script or carefully indexed representation for large grids; check row lengths and changed-cell coordinates before submission.
8. **Verify the final action.** Confirm dimensions, allowed values, exact row count and width, and that unchanged regions match the input. If submitting, output exactly one action with a valid grid. Do not claim correctness until the environment confirms it.

## Common pitfalls

- **Premature pattern naming:** an L-shaped marker and nearby object may suggest a familiar rule, but proximity alone is weak evidence. Compare with similar unchanged candidates.
- **Ignoring changed-cell precision:** output examples often differ at just one component; changing too much is a common failure.
- **Single-example overfit:** a rule that fits one demo may not generalize; leverage additional demos to distinguish selection from coincidence.
- **Coordinate drift:** grids are often wide or tall; keep row/column indexing consistent (state whether zero- or one-based) and validate dimensions mechanically where practical.
- **Tool overhead:** parallel analysis can help on genuinely ambiguous hypotheses, but repeated status checks and redundant delegation do not improve the puzzle evidence. Prefer independent, bounded analyses that return a concrete candidate and rationale.

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks with colored integer grids and a small number of input/output demonstrations. Infer the simplest rule that explains every demonstrated change, then apply it exactly to the test grid.

## Workflow

1. **Preserve the interaction contract.** If the environment requires one action per turn (submit/request_demo/finish), emit exactly one valid action object in the required location. Do not add explanatory text when the protocol requires JSON-only. Respect attempt and demo caps.
2. **Parse the grid before hypothesizing.** Record dimensions, background color, connected components by color (usually 4-connectivity; also inspect diagonal relationships), bounding boxes, shapes, and repeated motifs. Watch for objects touching the boundary or separated by only one background cell.
3. **Use demonstrations as before/after diffs.** For every demo, identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed invariant. Group changed cells into components; note whether objects are recolored, moved, copied, extended, or deleted. Never summarize an entire demo as a vague scene description.
4. **Infer candidate rules from relations, not just resemblance.** Compare the changed object against unchanged objects of the same color/shape. Test plausible selectors (orientation, position relative to an anchor, size, shape, count, alignment, enclosure, matching dimensions) against all demos. Explicitly identify counterexamples and eliminate hypotheses that fail them.
5. **Treat multiple demos as constraints.** The rule should explain each example with the same mechanism, allowing only task-intrinsic variation such as colors, orientations, or object positions. If two explanations remain plausible and would yield different test outputs, ask for another demo when its expected value exceeds its cost.
6. **Request demonstrations strategically.** A demo request costs one point, but a wrong submission also costs one and an unsolved instance may incur the full budget. Ask when it can distinguish specific live hypotheses; avoid requesting merely for reassurance after the rule is already strongly constrained. Before requesting, state internally which outcomes would confirm/reject each candidate.
7. **Apply transformations minimally.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and alter only cells compelled by the inferred rule. Preserve dimensions and all unrelated pixels. Use a small script or carefully indexed representation for large grids; check row lengths and changed-cell coordinates before submission.
8. **Verify the final action.** Confirm dimensions, allowed values, exact row count and width, and that unchanged regions match the input. If submitting, output exactly one action with a valid grid. Do not claim correctness until the environment confirms it.

## Common pitfalls

- **Premature pattern naming:** an L-shaped marker and nearby object may suggest a familiar rule, but proximity alone is weak evidence. Compare with similar unchanged candidates.
- **Ignoring changed-cell precision:** output examples often differ at just one component; changing too much is a common failure.
- **Single-example overfit:** a rule that fits one demo may not generalize; leverage additional demos to distinguish selection from coincidence.
- **Coordinate drift:** grids are often wide or tall; keep row/column indexing consistent (state whether zero- or one-based) and validate dimensions mechanically where practical.
- **Tool overhead:** parallel analysis can help on genuinely ambiguous hypotheses, but repeated status checks and redundant delegation do not improve the puzzle evidence. Prefer independent, bounded analyses that return a concrete candidate and rationale.

## Common pitfalls

- **Premature pattern naming:** an L-shaped marker and nearby object may suggest a familiar rule, but proximity alone is weak evidence. Compare with similar unchanged candidates.
- **Ignoring changed-cell precision:** output examples often differ at just one component; changing too much is a common failure.
- **Single-example overfit:** a rule that fits one demo may not generalize; leverage additional demos to distinguish selection from coincidence.
- **Coordinate drift:** grids are often wide or tall; keep row/column indexing consistent (state whether zero- or one-based) and validate dimensions mechanically where practical.
- **Tool overhead:** parallel analysis can help on genuinely ambiguous hypotheses, but repeated status checks and redundant delegation do not improve the puzzle evidence. Prefer independent, bounded analyses that return a concrete candidate and rationale.

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC-style colored-grid puzzle solving.

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC-style tasks with colored integer grids and a small number of input/output demonstrations. Infer the simplest rule that explains every demonstrated change, then apply it exactly to the test grid.

## Workflow

1. **Preserve the interaction contract.** If the environment requires one action per turn (submit/request_demo/finish), emit exactly one valid action object in the required location. Do not add explanatory text when the protocol requires JSON-only. Respect attempt and demo caps.
2. **Parse the grid before hypothesizing.** Record dimensions, background color, connected components by color (usually 4-connectivity; also inspect diagonal relationships), bounding boxes, shapes, and repeated motifs. Watch for objects touching the boundary or separated by only one background cell.
3. **Use demonstrations as before/after diffs.** For every demo, identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed invariant. Group changed cells into components; note whether objects are recolored, moved, copied, extended, or deleted. Never summarize an entire demo as a vague scene description.
4. **Infer candidate rules from relations, not just resemblance.** Compare the changed object against unchanged objects of the same color/shape. Test plausible selectors (orientation, position relative to an anchor, size, shape, count, alignment, enclosure, matching dimensions) against all demos. Explicitly identify counterexamples and eliminate hypotheses that fail them.
5. **Treat multiple demos as constraints.** The rule should explain each example with the same mechanism, allowing only task-intrinsic variation such as colors, orientations, or object positions. If two explanations remain plausible and would yield different test outputs, ask for another demo when its expected value exceeds its cost.
6. **Request demonstrations strategically.** A demo request costs one point, but a wrong submission also costs one and an unsolved instance may incur the full budget. Ask when it can distinguish specific live hypotheses; avoid requesting merely for reassurance after the rule is already strongly constrained. Before requesting, state internally which outcomes would confirm/reject each candidate.
7. **Apply transformations minimally.** Start from an exact copy of the test grid and alter only cells compelled by the inferred rule. Preserve dimensions and all unrelated pixels. Use a small script or carefully indexed representation for large grids; check row lengths and changed-cell coordinates before submission.
8. **Verify the final action.** Confirm dimensions, allowed values, exact row count and width, and that unchanged regions match the input. If submitting, output exactly one action with a valid grid. Do not claim correctness until the environment confirms it.

## Common pitfalls

- **Premature pattern naming:** an L-shaped marker and nearby object may suggest a familiar rule, but proximity alone is weak evidence. Compare with similar unchanged candidates.
- **Ignoring changed-cell precision:** output examples often differ at just one component; changing too much is a common failure.
- **Single-example overfit:** a rule that fits one demo may not generalize; leverage additional demos to distinguish selection from coincidence.
- **Coordinate drift:** grids are often wide or tall; keep row/column indexing consistent (state whether zero- or one-based) and validate dimensions mechanically where practical.
- **Tool overhead:** parallel analysis can help on genuinely ambiguous hypotheses, but repeated status checks and redundant delegation do not improve the puzzle evidence. Prefer independent, bounded analyses that return a concrete candidate and rationale.

## Support reference
